label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
read: RC2 70-page edition, draft: manuscript/rc2/70/ (17 files, the storyteller's new order) and its 61-page PDF built at 521f9e72
where_i_skimmed_or_stopped: 01: the voice-note quotations and the Bret Victor section are about slides and the editor, not my team; I skimmed to 'Do this now'.
02: four stops of screenshots of a site I cannot open from a phone; I took the Stop 4 idea (rules with the mistake behind each) and moved on.
06 and 07: good ideas (mail as files, 'To-' notes in commits) buried in commit hashes, times and the '@' anecdote; I skimmed the middle.
09 and 10: the afternoon asks table, the storyteller's tree and the minute-by-minute last ten minutes are a story first and a method second; I read for the hold only.
11 and 13: useful lists, but the three accounts of why he stopped and the handover chapter repeat what I had already understood.
17: a glossary at the back; I did not need it by then.
first_thing_i_would_do: Copy the one-page start list at the front: write a page of rules for my own agent, a hold file that names who lifts it, and a shared folder for requests between our team's agents, before the next planning meeting.
price: About 10 to 12 pounds as an ebook; I would pay 20 only if the front start page and the checklist were sold as a short companion I could hand to the team.
why: The method is real and copyable (brief, page of rules, check, hold, notes through files), and the failures kept in make it believable. But 61 pages of a one-day story is more than a busy team member will read; the takeaway is in about six pages. For my conference team the multi-person parts (shared brief, board, hold, who lifts it when the owner is away) are the point, and they are the thinnest: chapter 14 says plainly the third factory has not run. I would also want a page on cost, and one on how each of us keeps our own agent from colliding with another's.

by_chapter.why: A story about slides versus animation and one man's voice note; the takeaway for a team only arrives at the end. Strong opener for a talk audience, slow for someone who has agents already.
by_chapter.quote: I talked over my own pictures.

by_chapter.why: The best page for me: five steps, five boxes, nothing else. It should arrive before chapter 1, or be repeated on the back cover.
by_chapter.quote: If you want to start now, this page is all you need. The rest of this book is why it works.

by_chapter.why: A guided tour of screenshots; the dashboard-and-hold stop and the rules-with-their-mistakes stop earn it, the rest is a catalogue.
by_chapter.quote: A page of rules you can read like a short history of what went wrong.

by_chapter.why: First page of rules, brief, reality file, one check, the brake made in hour two. Concrete and copyable, with a shop owner's example I could adapt.
by_chapter.quote: A thing not listed here does not exist, whatever a brief or an article says.

by_chapter.why: Roles with a rule each and the mistake behind it; 'a scope is a setting, not a boundary' is the sentence a team should hear. The cast-with-voices device is charming but long.
by_chapter.quote: A scope is a setting, not a boundary: it catches mistakes, not a steered agent.

by_chapter.why: The five-step wake walked through one real record, including a partial and a finding, is the clearest picture of how a factory checks itself. The Wardley map at the end is lost on me.
by_chapter.quote: Partial is a true answer. Done would have been a nicer one.

by_chapter.why: Mail, board and commit notes as files is the part I would copy, but it is delivered through hashes and clock times. The letter-on-a-clock picture helps.
by_chapter.quote: A request is a file, and the answer is a file.

by_chapter.why: Two kinds of trigger and the 162-wakes chart are interesting; the long thread about one picture sent back three times is anecdote. 'If it is not in a file, it did not happen' is the takeaway.
by_chapter.quote: If it is not in a file, it did not happen.

by_chapter.why: Register, check, site, brief: four pipes, each a thing I can set up. Honest that the corrections file was never used.
by_chapter.quote: Gaps are allowed. Hiding them is not.

by_chapter.why: Port-not-rebuild is a good point for a team under time pressure, but it is wrapped in the afternoon's timeline, the storyteller's tree and the objection thread. Too many threads for one chapter.
The hold as one file with 'who lifts it' written in it is the single most useful idea for my team. The minute-by-minute lead-in is slower than it needs to be.
The failures at full size, each with a cost line, are what make the book trustworthy. The three explanations for why he stopped are more about the editor than about my team.
by_chapter.quote: A book about a factory that only shows what worked would be a brochure.

by_chapter.why: The honest security chapter: second reading is not a second identity; controls fail because nobody switches them on. Useful for deciding who sits outside our team.
by_chapter.quote: Most controls do not fail because someone defeats them. They fail because nobody gets round to switching them on.

by_chapter.why: Session versus member and the handover are the right idea, but the chapter sits late and repeats the status-and-debrief habit already in chapters 5 and 7.
by_chapter.quote: A session is not a member.

by_chapter.why: Closest to my situation: several people, each with their own agents, one brief, one board, one hold. But it is a plan, labelled as such, and the same three paragraphs are then repeated in the next section. I wanted the part that is not yet written.
by_chapter.quote: Everything in this section is a plan.

by_chapter.why: The five steps with what to do and what to check, plus the checklist and the last word, are the payoff. The checklist page is the thing I would print. Step text is dense, and chapter 16 repeats 01b.
by_chapter.quote: Ship something somebody else can use, then do it again.

by_chapter.why: A glossary that restates the word boxes. Fine as an appendix; I would not miss it.

pictures_that_help: p.4 and p.7: the A-to-B slide with speech bubbles beside the loop of see, ask, see again says the chapter in two seconds.
p.17 and p.18: the stack of files in the first two hours, and the team pattern card (one brief, one board, one hold, a page of rules per member).
p.23 and p.24: the wake clock and the five-box wake record with the finding highlighted.
p.30 to p.31: the 162-wakes card and the day-by-trigger bars.
p.33 to p.35: the register bar and the check card with ticks.
p.48: the running, held, released state diagram.
p.43: the hold file as a page, 'No member lifts it.'
p.45 and p.47: the failure cards, each with its cost.
p.54 and p.55: the second team's cast cards and the 'three people, one brief, one board, one hold' picture.
p.57 and p.60: the five-step path and the checklist page.
pictures_most_missed: p.9: 'Figure to come' for the one printable sheet of the five steps; this is the page my team would pin up, and it is the box I missed most.
p.50: 'Figure to come' for this book's team at the table with security's chair filled; a small loss.
p.49: 'Figure to come' for the empty chair beside the two inside reviewers; the chapter's argument needs it.
p.52: 'Figure to come' for two sessions of one member side by side; the handover idea needs it.
pages_too_tight: p.57 and p.58: the five steps with 'Rests on', 'What to do' and 'What to check' under each, in small type; the most important page of the book is the densest.
p.5 to p.7: the 'where this came from' notes in small type, plus long quotations, crowd the opening chapter.
p.31 and p.46: running text with hash-and-time detail at small size.
p.19 and p.20: the roles chapter is a wall of cast lines.
best_line: Nobody needs permission to stop. Everybody needs his to start again.
worst_moment: Chapter 14, where the three shared things are described twice in a row ('The third, planned' and 'What the three shared things need, day to day') and then marked 'a plan, not yet run': the section my team needs most is the one with no evidence behind it.
top_three_changes: Put the one-page start list (01b) first, drawn, not 'Figure to come', and cut or move chapters 1 and 2 behind it so the takeaway comes in the first five pages.

Make the several-people case concrete: a worked example of three people with their own agents, one brief, one board, who lifts the hold, and how two agents avoid changing the same file; merge the two plan sections in chapter 14.
Shorten the timeline-heavy chapters (6, 7, 9, 10) to the method and one scene each, and give the five-step pages in chapter 16 more room.
notes: I read this as a stand-and-talks team member would, with a short break between meetings: the method is sound and copyable, and the honest failures are the best part. The story is told at a length that suits a reader who already wants the story. Most of the takeaways are also in the 'Do this now' lines, which are very good; they alone would make a short guide. The book never says how much cost or how many people the first factory needed in terms I can budget.
